```{python}
import pandas as pd

# Live Google Sheet (switch back to this once the module is running):
# df = pd.read_csv("https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/e/2PACX-1vRWIOZ03GpUJgqvGVmI9cih169mMq0ajLMj6a0VTd2tytB3K5BmX5AUiKQ8FKIL6KUKEcgb-1LR-1eM/pub?gid=0&single=true&output=csv")
# Synthetic data for building/testing slides before the module runs:
df = pd.read_csv("data/synthetic_reaction_times.csv")

if 'name' in df.columns and 'student_name' not in df.columns:
    df = df.rename(columns={'name': 'student_name'})
if 'finger_mm' not in df.columns:
    df['finger_mm'] = None
df['finger_mm'] = pd.to_numeric(df['finger_mm'], errors='coerce')

student_summary = (
    df.groupby('student_name')
    .agg(mean_rt=('reaction_time_ms', 'mean'), device=('device', 'first'),
         caffeine=('caffeine', 'first'), finger_mm=('finger_mm', 'first'))
    .reset_index()
    .round(1)
)

# Individual trial-level rows for the live regressions below — one row per trial, not per student
trial_data = df[['reaction_time_ms', 'finger_mm', 'device', 'caffeine']].copy()

import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

# Real fitted model, used for both the raw statsmodels output and the booktabs table below.
# Individual trial-level reaction times (not student means) as the dependent variable.
reading_model = smf.ols("reaction_time_ms ~ finger_mm + device + caffeine", data=df).fit(cov_type="HC1")

_summary_lines = reading_model.summary().as_text().splitlines()
_cut = next(i for i, line in enumerate(_summary_lines) if line.startswith("Omnibus"))
reading_summary_text = "\n".join(_summary_lines[:_cut]).rstrip()

# Device interaction task — captured real output for the "What you should have found" reveal
interaction_model = smf.ols("reaction_time_ms ~ finger_mm * device", data=df).fit(cov_type="HC1")
_inter_lines = interaction_model.summary().as_text().splitlines()
_inter_cut = next(i for i, line in enumerate(_inter_lines) if line.startswith("Omnibus"))
interaction_summary_text = "\n".join(_inter_lines[:_inter_cut]).rstrip()

# OVB task — simple vs multiple, captured as a compact real params printout
simple_model = smf.ols("reaction_time_ms ~ finger_mm", data=df).fit(cov_type="HC1")
ovb_output_text = (
    ">>> print(simple.params.round(3))\n" + simple_model.params.round(3).to_string()
    + "\n\n>>> print(multi.params.round(3))\n" + reading_model.params.round(3).to_string()
)

# Categorical-variable task — captured real output
cat_model = smf.ols("reaction_time_ms ~ finger_mm + device", data=df).fit(cov_type="HC1")
_cat_lines = cat_model.summary().as_text().splitlines()
_cat_cut = next(i for i, line in enumerate(_cat_lines) if line.startswith("Omnibus"))
cat_summary_text = "\n".join(_cat_lines[:_cat_cut]).rstrip()

def _stars(p):
    return "***" if p < 0.01 else "**" if p < 0.05 else "*" if p < 0.1 else ""

_labels = {"finger_mm": "Finger length (mm)", "device[T.Phone]": "Device: Phone",
           "caffeine[T.Yes]": "Caffeine: Yes", "Intercept": "Constant"}
_order = ["finger_mm", "device[T.Phone]", "caffeine[T.Yes]", "Intercept"]

results_df = pd.DataFrame(
    [{"Variable": _labels[_name],
      "Coefficient": f"{reading_model.params[_name]:.2f}{_stars(reading_model.pvalues[_name])}",
      "Std. Error": f"({reading_model.bse[_name]:.2f})"}
     for _name in _order]
    + [{"Variable": "N", "Coefficient": str(int(reading_model.nobs)), "Std. Error": ""},
       {"Variable": "R²", "Coefficient": f"{reading_model.rsquared:.3f}", "Std. Error": ""}]
)
results_markdown = results_df.to_markdown(index=False)

booktabs_rows = [
    {"label": _labels[_name],
     "coef": f"{reading_model.params[_name]:.2f}{_stars(reading_model.pvalues[_name])}",
     "se": f"({reading_model.bse[_name]:.2f})"}
    for _name in _order
]
booktabs_n = int(reading_model.nobs)
booktabs_r2 = round(reading_model.rsquared, 3)

# Gender pay gap case study — Bekes & Kezdi's own CPS earnings dataset (N=149,316 nationally),
# filtered here to the same sample as Ch10: graduate degree, age 24-65, 20+ usual weekly hours.
# Downloaded from https://osf.io/g8p9j/ (their public data repo) and filtered once, offline.
cps_df = pd.read_csv("data/cps_gender_pay_gap.csv")

gap_m1 = smf.ols("ln_wage ~ female", data=cps_df).fit(cov_type="HC1")
gap_m2 = smf.ols("ln_wage ~ female + C(education, Treatment('MA'))", data=cps_df).fit(cov_type="HC1")
gap_m3 = smf.ols("ln_wage ~ female + C(education, Treatment('PhD'))", data=cps_df).fit(cov_type="HC1")

def _gap_cell(model, name):
    if name not in model.params.index:
        return ""
    return f"{model.params[name]:.3f}{_stars(model.pvalues[name])}"

gap_rows = [
    {"variable": "female", "m1": _gap_cell(gap_m1, "female"), "m2": _gap_cell(gap_m2, "female"), "m3": _gap_cell(gap_m3, "female")},
    {"variable": "ed_Professional", "m1": "", "m2": _gap_cell(gap_m2, "C(education, Treatment('MA'))[T.Professional]"), "m3": _gap_cell(gap_m3, "C(education, Treatment('PhD'))[T.Professional]")},
    {"variable": "ed_PhD", "m1": "", "m2": _gap_cell(gap_m2, "C(education, Treatment('MA'))[T.PhD]"), "m3": ""},
    {"variable": "ed_MA", "m1": "", "m2": "", "m3": _gap_cell(gap_m3, "C(education, Treatment('PhD'))[T.MA]")},
    {"variable": "Constant", "m1": _gap_cell(gap_m1, "Intercept"), "m2": _gap_cell(gap_m2, "Intercept"), "m3": _gap_cell(gap_m3, "Intercept")},
]
gap_n = int(gap_m1.nobs)

# Interaction: does the gender gap itself change with age?
gap_inter = smf.ols("ln_wage ~ female * age", data=cps_df).fit(cov_type="HC1")

gap_inter_rows = [
    {"variable": "female", "value": _gap_cell(gap_inter, "female")},
    {"variable": "age", "value": _gap_cell(gap_inter, "age")},
    {"variable": "female × age", "value": _gap_cell(gap_inter, "female:age")},
    {"variable": "Constant", "value": _gap_cell(gap_inter, "Intercept")},
]

_age_grid = list(range(24, 65))
_a0, _b_age, _b_f, _b_fage = (gap_inter.params["Intercept"], gap_inter.params["age"],
                              gap_inter.params["female"], gap_inter.params["female:age"])
gap_age_lines = (
    [{"age": a, "ln_wage": _a0 + _b_age * a, "group": "Men"} for a in _age_grid]
    + [{"age": a, "ln_wage": (_a0 + _b_f) + (_b_age + _b_fage) * a, "group": "Women"} for a in _age_grid]
)

# NaN is not valid JSON — clean before ojs_define
student_summary_clean = student_summary.astype(object).where(student_summary.notna(), None)
trial_data_clean = trial_data.astype(object).where(trial_data.notna(), None)

ojs_define(
    student_summary      = student_summary_clean.to_dict(orient='records'),
    trial_data            = trial_data_clean.to_dict(orient='records'),
    reading_summary_text = reading_summary_text,
    interaction_summary_text = interaction_summary_text,
    ovb_output_text       = ovb_output_text,
    cat_summary_text      = cat_summary_text,
    results_markdown      = results_markdown,
    booktabs_rows         = booktabs_rows,
    booktabs_n            = booktabs_n,
    booktabs_r2           = booktabs_r2,
    gap_rows               = gap_rows,
    gap_n                   = gap_n,
    gap_inter_rows          = gap_inter_rows,
    gap_age_lines           = gap_age_lines,
)
```

```{ojs}
  // Sets each wrapper's correct starting state immediately, including on a
  // reload or direct navigation to a slide whose fragment is already shown

  document.querySelectorAll('.shrink-on-reveal[data-frag]').forEach(el => {
    const frag = document.getElementById(el.dataset.frag)
    el.classList.toggle('is-small', !!frag?.classList.contains('visible'))

    wrapperFor(event.fragment.id)?.classList.add('is-small')
  })
  Reveal.on('fragmenthidden', (event) => {
    wrapperFor(event.fragment.id)?.classList.remove('is-small')
  })
```

```{ojs}
olsFit = function(X, y) {
  const n = X.length, k = X[0].length + 1
  const design = X.map(row => [1, ...row])
  const XtX = Array.from({length: k}, (_, i) => Array.from({length: k}, (_, j) => d3.sum(design.map(r => r[i] * r[j]))))
  const Xty = Array.from({length: k}, (_, i) => d3.sum(design.map((r, idx) => r[i] * y[idx])))
  const A = XtX.map((row, i) => [...row, Xty[i]])
  for (let col = 0; col < k; col++) {
    let piv = col
    for (let r = col + 1; r < k; r++) if (Math.abs(A[r][col]) > Math.abs(A[piv][col])) piv = r
    const tmp = A[col]; A[col] = A[piv]; A[piv] = tmp
    for (let r = 0; r < k; r++) {
      if (r === col) continue
      const factor = A[r][col] / A[col][col]
      for (let c = col; c <= k; c++) A[r][c] -= factor * A[col][c]
    }
  }
  const coefs = A.map((row, i) => row[k] / row[i])
  const fitted = design.map(r => d3.sum(r.map((v, i) => v * coefs[i])))
  const resid = y.map((yi, i) => yi - fitted[i])
  return { coefs, fitted, resid, n, k }
}
```

## {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {style="text-align: center; padding-top: 180px;"}
[**Multiple regression**]{style="font-size: 2.2em; color: white;"}

[Finger length alone barely moved the needle. What if device or caffeine matter too — and are tangled up with finger length itself?]{style="font-size: 1.1em; color: #aaa; padding-top: 20px; display: block;"}
:::

## One x at a time was never the whole story

::: {.instructions-box}
HR has separate regressions: reaction time on finger length, reaction time on device. Someone asks: which one actually matters?
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Naive answer:** run each regression separately, compare the slopes, done.

**Why it's not that simple:** if finger length and device happen to be correlated in our sample — say, one device tends to attract a particular hand-size group — each regression is silently absorbing some of the other variable's effect. We can't tell which x is doing the work until we ask both questions at once.
:::

---

## Why more than one x?

---

## Three reasons to add a second x

- **Broader patterns** — plain exploratory work, understanding the data more fully
- **Closer to comparing similar observations** — holding one variable fixed while looking at another gets nearer to *ceteris paribus*, "all else equal"
- **Better prediction** — more of the variation in y gets explained

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## Two x variables

$$y^E = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2$$

- $\beta_1$: the difference in average y across observations that differ in $x_1$ **but share the same $x_2$**
- $\beta_2$: the same idea, the other way round
- We can now compare observations that are similar in one explanatory variable, to isolate what the other one is doing

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## Reading real output

From here on, every regression we show comes with the code that produced it. We'll assume the data's already clean — the focus is the model-fitting call and how to read what comes back.

```{.python}
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

model = smf.ols('reaction_time_ms ~ finger_mm + device', data=df).fit(cov_type='HC1')
print(model.summary())
```

::: {.fragment}
`cov_type='HC1'` — heteroskedasticity-robust SE, the Week 5 default, carried forward as standard practice.
:::

---

## Omitted variable bias

---

## Comparing the simple and multiple slope

$$y^E = \alpha + \beta x_1 \qquad\qquad y^E = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2$$

An intermediate step — regress $x_2$ on $x_1$ itself, slope $\delta$:

$$x_2^E = \gamma + \delta x_1$$

::: {.fragment}
Substituting back in gives a precise relationship between the two versions of the $x_1$ slope:

$$\beta - \beta_1 = \delta\beta_2$$
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## Omitted variable bias, named

$$\beta - \beta_1 = \delta\beta_2$$

- This gap is the **omitted variable bias (OVB)**
- If you care about $\beta_1$, the simple regression $y^E=\alpha+\beta x_1$ is **the wrong regression** — it omits $x_2$
- The bias is exactly zero only if $x_1$ and $x_2$ are uncorrelated ($\delta=0$), or $x_2$ has no effect on y in the full model ($\beta_2=0$)

::: {.fragment}
Neither condition is something you can assume — it has to be checked, or reasoned about.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## Worked example: beer sales and price {.smaller}

::: {.instructions-box}
A scenario where we can control the truth: monthly change in **our** log price ($x_1$) and a **competitor's** log price ($x_2$) tend to move together, both driving change in log sales (y). Simulate it, and check the OVB formula holds exactly.
:::

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
competitor_price = rng.normal(0, 2.0, 300)
our_price        = 0.8 * competitor_price + rng.normal(0, 1.2, 300)   # correlated with competitor's
sales            = -3*our_price + 3*competitor_price + rng.normal(0, 2.5, 300)  # true betas: -3, +3
df = pd.DataFrame({'sales': sales, 'our_price': our_price, 'competitor_price': competitor_price})

simple = smf.ols('sales ~ our_price', data=df).fit()
multi  = smf.ols('sales ~ our_price + competitor_price', data=df).fit()
aux    = smf.ols('competitor_price ~ our_price', data=df).fit()   # x2 on x1, per the formula above
```

```{python}
#| output: asis
import numpy as np

_rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
_competitor_price = _rng.normal(0, 2.0, 300)
_our_price        = 0.8 * _competitor_price + _rng.normal(0, 1.2, 300)
_sales            = -3*_our_price + 3*_competitor_price + _rng.normal(0, 2.5, 300)
_sim_df = pd.DataFrame({'sales': _sales, 'our_price': _our_price, 'competitor_price': _competitor_price})

_simple = smf.ols('sales ~ our_price', data=_sim_df).fit()
_multi  = smf.ols('sales ~ our_price + competitor_price', data=_sim_df).fit()
_aux    = smf.ols('competitor_price ~ our_price', data=_sim_df).fit()

_beta   = _simple.params['our_price']
_beta1  = _multi.params['our_price']
_beta2  = _multi.params['competitor_price']
_delta  = _aux.params['our_price']

_lines = (
    f"beta&nbsp;(simple)&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;=&nbsp;{_beta:.3f}<br>"
    f"beta1&nbsp;(multiple)&nbsp;&nbsp;=&nbsp;{_beta1:.3f}<br>"
    f"beta2&nbsp;(multiple)&nbsp;&nbsp;=&nbsp;{_beta2:.3f}<br>"
    f"delta&nbsp;(x2&nbsp;on&nbsp;x1)&nbsp;&nbsp;=&nbsp;{_delta:.3f}"
)
print(
    '::: {style="font-family: monospace; font-size: 0.85em; background: #f8f8f8; '
    'border-left: 4px solid #457b9d; padding: 14px 20px; border-radius: 4px; line-height: 1.9;"}\n'
    f'{_lines}\n:::'
)
```

::: {.fragment}
```{python}
#| output: asis
_lhs = _beta - _beta1
_rhs = _delta * _beta2
print(
    '::: {style="font-family: monospace; font-size: 0.85em; text-align:center; margin-top: 8px;"}\n'
    f'beta&nbsp;−&nbsp;beta1&nbsp;=&nbsp;{_lhs:.4f}&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;delta×beta2&nbsp;=&nbsp;{_rhs:.4f}\n:::'
)
```

The two sides match **exactly** —  $\hat\beta-\hat\beta_1$ and $\hat\delta\hat\beta_2$ are the same calculation, done two different ways. And since we built this dataset ourselves, we know the simple regression really is biased: the true effect of our own price is $-3$, but $\hat\beta$ lands nowhere near it — because it's silently absorbing the competitor-price effect too, through the correlation between the two.
:::

## Language: conditioning, controlling, confounding

- We measure differences in y by $x_1$, **conditional on** $x_2$ — or **controlling for** $x_2$
- When a variable that belongs in the model is left out, it's an **omitted variable**
- If it's correlated with both $x_1$ and y, it's a **confounder** — the slope on $x_1$ is *confounded*

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

---

## Multicollinearity — a different problem

---

## Multicollinearity, defined

::: {.instructions-box}
**Multicollinearity**: two or more explanatory variables in the same regression are strongly correlated with *each other*.
:::

- It does **not** bias any coefficient — β̂ is still right, on average
- It **inflates the standard errors** — β̂ becomes imprecise, harder to pin down
- Intuition: if $x_1$ and $x_2$ move together almost every time, there's barely any data where one is high and the other is low — and that's exactly the comparison OLS needs to estimate their separate slopes

::: {.fragment}
Contrast with Section B: **OVB is about what's missing** from the model. **Multicollinearity is about what's already in it**, just tangled together.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## Where the standard error comes from

$$SE(\hat\beta_1) = \frac{Std[e]}{\sqrt{n}\cdot Std[x_1]\cdot\sqrt{1-R_1^2}}$$

- Same ingredients as Week 5's simple-regression SE — fit, spread of $x_1$, sample size
- **New**: $R_1^2$ — the R² from regressing $x_1$ on $x_2$ (and any other x's). The more $x_1$ is *explained by* the other regressors, the bigger this term, the bigger the SE

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## Perfect vs. imperfect collinearity

- **Perfect collinearity** — $x_1$ is an exact linear function of $x_2$. Coefficients literally can't be calculated; software drops one variable for you
- **Multicollinearity** — strong but *imperfect* correlation between explanatory variables. Coefficients and SEs can still be computed — but the SEs may be large

::: {.fragment}
Intuition: multicollinearity means there aren't many observations that differ in $x_1$ while staying similar in $x_2$ — so there's little clean information left to estimate $\beta_1$ precisely.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## See it happen

```{ojs}
viewof corrSlider = {
  const f = html`<div style="display:flex;align-items:center;gap:14px;font-size:13px;
                              font-family:'Helvetica Neue',sans-serif;padding:4px 2px;color:#333;">
    <span style="color:#666;white-space:nowrap;">Correlation between x₁ and x₂</span>
    <input type="range" min="0" max="0.98" step="0.02" value="0"
           style="width:200px;cursor:pointer;accent-color:#e63946;">
    <span id="cs-label" style="font-weight:700;min-width:36px;color:#e63946;">0.00</span>
  </div>`
  const slider = f.querySelector('input')
  const label  = f.querySelector('#cs-label')
  slider.addEventListener('input', () => {
    label.textContent = (+slider.value).toFixed(2)
    f.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('input'))
  })
  Object.defineProperty(f, 'value', { get: () => +slider.value })
  return f
}
```

```{ojs}
{
  const n = 200
  const seed = i => { const s = Math.sin(i * 12.9898) * 43758.5453; return (s - Math.floor(s)) * 2 - 1 }
  const seed2 = i => { const s = Math.sin(i * 78.233) * 12345.6789; return (s - Math.floor(s)) * 2 - 1 }
  const x1 = d3.range(n).map(i => seed(i))
  const x2 = d3.range(n).map(i => corrSlider * x1[i] + Math.sqrt(1 - corrSlider ** 2) * seed2(i))
  const y = d3.range(n).map(i => 2 * x1[i] + 1.5 * x2[i] + seed2(i * 3.1))
  const fitFor = c => {
    const x2c = d3.range(n).map(i => c * x1[i] + Math.sqrt(1 - c ** 2) * seed2(i))
    const model = olsFit(x1.map((v, i) => [v, x2c[i]]), y)
    const sdE = Math.sqrt(d3.sum(model.resid.map(e => e ** 2)) / (n - model.k))
    const sdX1 = Math.sqrt(d3.mean(x1.map(v => (v - d3.mean(x1)) ** 2)))
    const auxR2 = (() => {
      const aux = olsFit(x2c.map(v => [v]), x1)
      const ybar = d3.mean(x1)
      const varY = d3.mean(x1.map(v => (v - ybar) ** 2))
      const varYhat = d3.mean(aux.fitted.map(f => (f - ybar) ** 2))
      return varYhat / varY
    })()
    return sdE / (Math.sqrt(n) * sdX1 * Math.sqrt(1 - auxR2))
  }
  const curve = d3.range(0, 0.99, 0.02).map(c => ({ c, se: fitFor(c) }))
  const currentSE = fitFor(corrSlider)
  const chart = Plot.plot({
    height: 320, marginLeft: 60,
    x: { label: "correlation between x₁ and x₂" }, y: { label: "SE(β̂₁)" },
    marks: [
      Plot.line(curve, { x: "c", y: "se", stroke: "#457b9d", strokeWidth: 2 }),
      Plot.dot([{ c: corrSlider, se: currentSE }], { x: "c", y: "se", fill: "#e63946", r: 6 }),
    ]
  })
  return html`<div>${chart}<p style="font-family:sans-serif;font-size:1em;text-align:center;">SE(β̂₁) at this correlation: <strong>${currentSE.toFixed(3)}</strong></p></div>`
}
```

::: {.instructions-box}
Simulated data, true coefficients fixed throughout. Drag the correlation up. The point estimate barely changes — but watch the SE climb, slowly at first, then sharply as correlation approaches 1.
:::

## Naming it: VIF

Software usually calls this number the **Variance Inflation Factor**:

$$VIF_k = \frac{1}{1-R_k^2}$$

- The exact same $R_k^2$ from two slides ago — just flipped into one number per variable
- Common rule of thumb: **VIF > 10** flags a real problem (some use a stricter >5)
- One line in `statsmodels`: `variance_inflation_factor(X, k)`



## VIF on our own data

```{ojs}
{
  const rows = trial_data.filter(d => d.finger_mm != null && !isNaN(d.finger_mm) && d.device != null && d.caffeine != null)
  const fm = rows.map(d => d.finger_mm)
  const dv = rows.map(d => d.device === "Phone" ? 1 : 0)
  const cf = rows.map(d => d.caffeine === "Yes" ? 1 : 0)
  const r2 = (y, X) => {
    const model = olsFit(X, y)
    const ybar = d3.mean(y)
    const varY = d3.mean(y.map(v => (v - ybar) ** 2))
    const varYhat = d3.mean(model.fitted.map(f => (f - ybar) ** 2))
    return varYhat / varY
  }
  const vif = (y, X) => 1 / (1 - r2(y, X))
  const rows3 = [
    { label: "Finger length", vif: vif(fm, dv.map((v, i) => [v, cf[i]])) },
    { label: "Device", vif: vif(dv, fm.map((v, i) => [v, cf[i]])) },
    { label: "Caffeine", vif: vif(cf, fm.map((v, i) => [v, dv[i]])) },
  ]
  return html`<table style="margin:0 auto;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:1.1em;border-collapse:collapse;">
    <tr style="border-bottom:2px solid #1a1a2e;"><th style="padding:8px 24px;text-align:left;">Variable</th><th style="padding:8px 24px;">VIF</th></tr>
    ${rows3.map(d => `<tr style="border-bottom:1px solid #ddd;"><td style="padding:6px 24px;">${d.label}</td><td style="padding:6px 24px;text-align:center;font-weight:700;">${d.vif.toFixed(2)}</td></tr>`).join('')}
  </table>`
}
```

::: {.instructions-box}
All close to 1 — finger length, device, and caffeine barely overlap in what they explain. That's why the Section B check earlier showed the finger-length coefficient barely moving: there was never much multicollinearity here to begin with, just weak signal.
:::

## The VIF trap

::: {.instructions-box}
A high VIF does **not** mean "drop this variable." If it's a genuine confounder, dropping it to fix a *precision* problem reintroduces the *bias* problem from Section B — often a worse trade.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The honest response to a high VIF is usually: report it, keep the variable if the causal story needs it, and be upfront that the estimate is imprecise. VIF is a diagnostic, not a decision rule.
:::

## What to actually do about it

- Look at pairwise correlations (or a correlation heatmap) early, before modelling
- Drop one of a highly correlated pair, or combine them (average, or a z-score index)
- Mostly a **small-sample problem** — hundreds to a few thousand observations
- With many x's: check $R_k^2$ for each variable regressed on all the others; drop if very high

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## The distinction that matters

|  | Omitted variable bias | Multicollinearity |
|---|---|---|
| **What it is** | Leaving out a variable that belongs in the model | Including two variables that are strongly correlated |
| **What it breaks** | The point estimate itself — wrong on average | Precision — the estimate is right on average, just noisy |
| **Does more data fix it?** | No. Same bias at any sample size | Yes. More data narrows the SE back down |
| **Direction known?** | Depends on $\delta$ and $\beta_2$ — could go either way | N/A — SE inflates, doesn't shift the estimate |

::: {.fragment}
Confusing these two is the single most common mistake in reading regression output. One is a bias problem you fix by *adding* the right variable. The other is a precision problem you sometimes fix by *removing* one.
:::

---

## Testing more than one coefficient

---

## Individual coefficients — same as before

Each $\hat\beta_k$ gets its own CI and t-test, exactly as in Week 5:

$$CI(\hat\beta_k)_{95\%} = \hat\beta_k \pm 2\,SE(\hat\beta_k) \qquad\qquad t=\frac{\hat\beta_k}{SE(\hat\beta_k)}$$

The only change is where $SE(\hat\beta_k)$ comes from — the formula with the $\sqrt{1-R_k^2}$ term from Section C.

## Testing several coefficients together

Sometimes the question isn't about one coefficient, but a *group* of them — e.g. "are all the geography dummies jointly zero?"

::: {.instructions-box}
The **F-test** answers this. Individually, none of the coefficients might be statistically distinguishable from zero — but jointly, they might still be.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The **global F-test** — are *all* slope coefficients zero? — is reported by default in most software. Gabor & Kézdi's own advice: don't lean on it too heavily. R² tells you almost the same thing, more simply, for that particular question.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## The full output, F-test included {.smaller}

```{.python}
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

model = smf.ols('reaction_time_ms ~ finger_mm + device + caffeine', data=df).fit(cov_type='HC1')
print(model.summary())
```

```{ojs}
html`<pre style="font-family:'SF Mono','Menlo',monospace;font-size:0.38em;line-height:1.25;
                  background:#f6f6f8;border:1px solid #e0e0e6;border-radius:6px;
                  padding:6px 14px;overflow-x:auto;white-space:pre;">${reading_summary_text}</pre>`
```

::: {.instructions-box}
`Prob (F-statistic) = 0.115` — can't reject that all three slopes are jointly zero. 200 rows looks like a lot, but it's really only 20 students × 10 repeated trials each — since finger length, device, and caffeine don't change trial-to-trial, the coefficients are identical to what you'd get averaging each student down to one row first. Same multicollinearity warning as Section C, flagged again at the bottom.
:::

Pull the real numbers straight off the fitted model into a small results table, then let pandas do the formatting:

```{.python}
def stars(p):
    return "***" if p < 0.01 else "**" if p < 0.05 else "*" if p < 0.1 else ""

results_df = pd.DataFrame(
    [{"Variable": label,
      "Coefficient": f"{model.params[name]:.2f}{stars(model.pvalues[name])}",
      "Std. Error": f"({model.bse[name]:.2f})"}
     for name, label in labels.items()]
    + [{"Variable": "N", "Coefficient": str(int(model.nobs)), "Std. Error": ""},
       {"Variable": "R²", "Coefficient": f"{model.rsquared:.3f}", "Std. Error": ""}]
)
print(results_df.to_markdown(index=False))
```

## Categorical variables, properly

---

## k categories, k − 1 dummies

A categorical x with values low/medium/high becomes two binary variables — one category left out as the **reference**:

$$y^E = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{medium} + \beta_2 x_{high}$$

- $\beta_0$ — average y in the reference category (low)
- $\beta_1$ — difference between medium and low
- $\beta_2$ — difference between high and low

::: {.fragment}
Include all *k* dummies (no reference left out) and you get the **dummy variable trap** — perfect collinearity with the intercept, and the model can't be estimated.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## Choosing a reference category

- **Substantive guide** — pick whatever you naturally want everything else compared to (the home market, the base product, the lowest tier)
- **Statistical guide** — pick a category with plenty of observations. A thin reference category means *every* comparison against it inherits a large SE

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## Real worked example: the gender pay gap

Log wage regressed on gender and graduate-degree category. 

```{.python}
cps_df = pd.read_csv("cps_gender_pay_gap.csv")

smf.ols('ln_wage ~ female', data=cps_df).fit(cov_type='HC1')                                    # (1)
smf.ols('ln_wage ~ female + C(education, Treatment("MA"))', data=cps_df).fit(cov_type='HC1')    # (2), ref = MA
smf.ols('ln_wage ~ female + C(education, Treatment("PhD"))', data=cps_df).fit(cov_type='HC1')   # (3), ref = PhD
```

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10. Data: `cps-earnings`, osf.io/g8p9j, 2014 CPS MORG (NBER), filtered to graduate-degree holders aged 24–65 working 20+ hours/week — the same restriction the textbook applies.
:::

## Interactions: different slopes for different groups

---

## When the pattern itself varies by group

An **interaction** asks: does the relationship between y and $x_1$ differ depending on a second variable, D? D is sometimes called a **moderator**.

::: {.fragment}
Examples: does customer rating relate to hotel price differently by star category? Does a drug's effect vary with patient age? Does the finger-length/reaction-time pattern differ by device?
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## The structural model

$$y^E = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 D + \beta_3\,(x_1 \times D)$$

- When $D=0$: $y^E = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1$ — intercept $\beta_0$, slope $\beta_1$
- When $D=1$: $y^E = (\beta_0+\beta_2) + (\beta_1+\beta_3)\,x_1$ — intercept shifts by $\beta_2$, slope shifts by $\beta_3$

::: {.fragment}
$\beta_3$ **is** the answer to the interaction question — literally the difference in slopes between the two groups. It gets its own SE, its own t-stat, its own CI, exactly like any other coefficient.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## Plotting it

```{.python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
colors = {'Laptop': '#457b9d', 'Phone': '#e63946'}

for device, group in df.groupby('device'):
    ax.scatter(group['finger_mm'], group['reaction_time_ms'],
               alpha=0.4, color=colors[device], label=device)

x_grid = np.linspace(df['finger_mm'].min(), df['finger_mm'].max(), 50)
for device in colors:
    pred = model.predict(pd.DataFrame({'finger_mm': x_grid, 'device': device}))
    ax.plot(x_grid, pred, color=colors[device], linewidth=2.5)

ax.set_xlabel('Finger length (mm)')
ax.set_ylabel('Reaction time (ms)')
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

::: {.instructions-box}
`model.predict()` on a small grid of finger-length values is the key move — it applies the fitted coefficients (and the categorical encoding) for you, so the fitted lines are guaranteed to match the regression exactly, not redrawn by hand.
:::

## The figure

```{ojs}
{
  const rows = trial_data.filter(d => d.finger_mm != null && !isNaN(d.finger_mm) && d.device != null)
  if (rows.length < 8) return html`<p style="color:#aaa;">Not enough data yet.</p>`
  const x = rows.map(d => d.finger_mm), y = rows.map(d => d.reaction_time_ms)
  const dev = rows.map(d => d.device === "Phone" ? 1 : 0)
  const inter = x.map((v, i) => v * dev[i])
  const model = olsFit(x.map((v, i) => [v, dev[i], inter[i]]), y)
  const xbar = d3.mean(x)
  const grid = d3.range(d3.min(x), d3.max(x), (d3.max(x) - d3.min(x)) / 40)
  const laptopLine = grid.map(v => ({ finger_mm: v, fit: model.coefs[0] + model.coefs[1] * v, group: "Laptop" }))
  const phoneLine = grid.map(v => ({ finger_mm: v, fit: model.coefs[0] + model.coefs[2] + (model.coefs[1] + model.coefs[3]) * v, group: "Phone" }))
  const chart = Plot.plot({
    height: 360, marginLeft: 60,
    x: { label: "Finger length (mm)" }, y: { label: "Reaction time (ms)" },
    color: { legend: true, domain: ["Laptop", "Phone"], range: ["#457b9d", "#e63946"] },
    marks: [
      Plot.dot(rows, { x: "finger_mm", y: "reaction_time_ms", stroke: d => d.device === "Phone" ? "#e63946" : "#457b9d", fill: "white", fillOpacity: 0.5, r: 2.5 }),
      Plot.line(laptopLine, { x: "finger_mm", y: "fit", stroke: "group", strokeWidth: 2.5 }),
      Plot.line(phoneLine, { x: "finger_mm", y: "fit", stroke: "group", strokeWidth: 2.5 }),
    ]
  })
  return html`<div>${chart}<p style="font-family:sans-serif;font-size:1em;text-align:center;">Interaction term (finger_mm × Phone): <strong>${model.coefs[3].toFixed(2)}</strong></p></div>`
}
```

::: {.instructions-box}
If the two lines are nearly parallel, the interaction term will be close to zero — the finger-length pattern doesn't meaningfully depend on device. If they visibly fan apart, it does.
:::

## Our own data hits its limit

::: {.instructions-box}
20 students, 200 trials — even a real interaction would be hard to detect at this scale, and a weak or noisy one is essentially invisible against sampling noise this size.
:::

::: {.fragment}
To actually *see* an interaction at work, we need a dataset with enough power to show one. Back to the CPS earnings data from Section E — 18,241 people, real signal, real stakes.
:::

## Does a near-zero coefficient mean no gap?

::: {.instructions-box}
`female` = −0.036, not even statistically distinguishable from zero (p ≈ 0.30). Does this mean the gender gap has disappeared? What does `female × age` = −0.003, strongly significant, tell you that the female coefficient alone doesn't?
:::

::: {.fragment}
Reread the structural model: at $D=1$ (female), the slope on age is $\beta_1+\beta_3$, not $\beta_1$. The "female" coefficient alone only describes the gap *at age zero* — a meaningless, never-observed point. The real story is in $\beta_3$.
:::

---

## Is it (more) causal?

---

## Ceteris paribus is a destination, not a guarantee

Conditioning on more variables gets us closer to comparing "apples to apples," even in observational data. But:

- *Ceteris paribus* means conditioning on **every** relevant confounder
- A regression can only condition on what's actually in the dataset, measured the way it happens to be measured
- **Conditioning on everything is impossible in general.** Multiple regression is hardly ever truly ceteris paribus

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## Not every correlated variable belongs

::: {.instructions-box}
Question: to see how TV advertising affects sales, should you control for how many people *viewed* the advert?
:::

::: {.fragment}
No. Fewer views is part of *why* less advertising hurts sales — it's not a confounder, it's a step in the causal chain itself. Controlling for it would control away the very thing you're trying to measure.
:::

::: {.fragment}
These are sometimes called **bad controls**. Telling a genuine confounder from a bad control by eye is genuinely hard — we'll get a proper diagram for reasoning about this in Week 9.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## Language, still

Even with five variables conditioned on, a regression is still a comparison of conditional means — not a randomized experiment.

::: {.instructions-box}
Same rule as Week 4: avoid "effect," avoid "increases/decreases," in observational data. "Higher finger length is associated with a difference of X ms, holding device and caffeine fixed" is honest. "Finger length affects reaction time" is not — not yet.
:::

---

## Prediction, overfitting, and choosing variables

---

## The ŷ–y plot

$$\hat y = \hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_1+\hat\beta_2x_2+\dots$$

A scatterplot of $\hat y$ (predicted) against actual y, with the 45° line:

- Points **right** of the line: overpredicted
- Points **left** of the line: underpredicted
- More informative than R² alone — it shows *where* the model struggles, not just how much

## Our own predictions vs. reality

```{ojs}
{
  const rows = trial_data.filter(d => d.finger_mm != null && !isNaN(d.finger_mm) && d.device != null && d.caffeine != null)
  if (rows.length < 6) return html`<p style="color:#aaa;">Not enough data yet.</p>`
  const x = rows.map(d => d.finger_mm), y = rows.map(d => d.reaction_time_ms)
  const dev = rows.map(d => d.device === "Phone" ? 1 : 0)
  const caf = rows.map(d => d.caffeine === "Yes" ? 1 : 0)
  const model = olsFit(x.map((v, i) => [v, dev[i], caf[i]]), y)
  const points = rows.map((d, i) => ({ yhat: model.fitted[i], y: d.reaction_time_ms }))
  const lo = Math.min(d3.min(points, d => d.yhat), d3.min(points, d => d.y))
  const hi = Math.max(d3.max(points, d => d.yhat), d3.max(points, d => d.y))
  return Plot.plot({
    height: 420, marginLeft: 60,
    x: { label: "predicted ŷ (ms)", domain: [lo - 10, hi + 10] },
    y: { label: "actual y (ms)", domain: [lo - 10, hi + 10] },
    marks: [
      Plot.line([{ x: lo - 10, y: lo - 10 }, { x: hi + 10, y: hi + 10 }], { x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "#ccc", strokeDasharray: "4,3" }),
      Plot.dot(points, { x: "yhat", y: "y", fill: "#1a1a2e", fillOpacity: 0.4, r: 3 }),
    ]
  })
}
```

::: {.instructions-box}
Points scattered tightly around the diagonal mean good predictions. Given how weak finger length's own relationship was, does this look like a model HR should rely on for individual predictions?
:::

## Overfitting and choosing variables

- **R² mechanically rises** every time you add a variable — even pure noise. It can never fall
- **Overfitting**: capturing patterns specific to this dataset that won't hold up elsewhere
- Purpose changes the rule: for a **causal** question, keep confounders that matter for comparison even if imprecise; for **prediction**, value simplicity and generalisability over fit

::: {.extension}
Rough sample-size guide (Gabor & Kézdi): 20–40 observations supports about 1–2 variables; 50–100 supports 2–4; a few hundred supports 5–10; a few thousand can support dozens, including dummies and interactions. Formal criteria like BIC penalise added variables directly — more in Week 10.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 10
:::

## Summary

- Multiple regression is a linear model with several x's, letting us compare observations that are similar in one variable while differing in another
- **Omitted variable bias** (leaving out a relevant, correlated variable) and **multicollinearity** (including two correlated variables) are opposite problems — bias vs. precision — and the fix for one is not the fix for the other
- It gets us closer to a causal comparison, never all the way there
- More variables always raises R² — that's not the same as a better model
